chunks: Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), so I said, 'What should the man say behind the Imam when he says, "Allah hears the one who praises Him"?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'He should say, "The Praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds," and he should lower his voice.'

key_terms.الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ: Al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-'alamin (The Praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds), the congregant's response
key_terms.خَلْفَ الْإِمَام: Khalfa al-imam (behind the Imam), referring to the position of the congregant in prayer
key_terms.سَمِعَ اللَّهُ لِمَنْ حَمِدَهُ: Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah (Allah hears the one who praises Him), the Imam's response to Al-hamdu lillah
key_terms.يَخْفِضُ مِنْ صَوْتِهِ: Yakhfidu min sawtihi (he lowers his voice), indicating the recitation is not loud (jahr) but quiet (khafi)

ai.seo_question: What should a worshipper say behind the Imam when he says Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi clarifies the specific liturgical response of the congregant (ma'mum) during the Imam's audible recitation of 'Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah', prescribing 'Al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-'alamin' to be recited quietly. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential distinction between the Imam's loud recitation in certain prayers and the congregant's quiet response, emphasizing the structural harmony of the prayer unit. The instruction to lower the voice ensures that the congregant's response does not disrupt the Imam's flow, reflecting the scholarly emphasis on order and humility in congregational worship.
